title: Lawyers in This State Are Allowed to Ghost Clients for Years. Why Don’t More Judges Stop Them?
author: Samantha Melamed
content:
One morning in July 2025, I was the lone spectator in Judge Frank Palumbo’s
courtroom in Philadelphia, watching prosecutors and public defenders haggle
over the fates of defendants.

Palumbo paused the proceedings to talk to a lawyer he’d appointed to help a
prisoner who had ineptly challenged his conviction. The lawyer profusely
thanked the judge for the job. Then, Palumbo offered a bit of guidance: “I
think I know where this is going to go. I don’t want to make it overly
complicated. It’s real simple.”

The judge said he’d pass along a brief that a different lawyer had filed
arguing that there was no merit to the man’s claims in a related case. “I’m
not saying plagiarize,” the judge said.

The attorney told the judge he got the message. “So it’s called a Finley
letter,” he said, using the common legal term for that no-merit brief, in
which an attorney can argue against the client’s claims and ask to withdraw
from the case.

“It’s looking like it’s going to be a Finley dismissal,” the judge agreed
after a bit more discussion, “but every option is open.”

I’ve spent years covering criminal justice in Pennsylvania, including the
post-conviction system that allows people to argue that their lawyer had
mishandled their case or to raise newly discovered evidence. That day, I left
the courtroom wondering how what I’d observed squared with the state’s promise
of effective legal representation in cases like this.

That question sent me on a yearlong reporting odyssey, during which I read
hundreds of Finley letters, tracked down court financial records from all 67
Pennsylvania counties, interviewed dozens of lawyers and analyzed thousands of
court dockets. What I wanted to know was: Why has it become the norm for
Pennsylvania’s lawyers to argue against their own clients? And who is this
system serving?

I found that lax rules, low pay and heavy caseloads have compromised legal
representation under the state’s Post Conviction Relief Act. Over the past
year, I’ve reported on how lawyers, working under fee structures banned in
other states, fell years behind on their cases. I spoke with prisoners who’d
[waited nearly a decade](https://www.propublica.org/article/post-conviction-
legal-delays-pennsylvania) for their lawyers to file anything and others whose
lawyers filed Finley letters [despite compelling evidence of
innocence](https://www.propublica.org/article/conviction-challenges-
philadelphia-law). I also looked at three years’ worth of invoices and found
that, three quarters of the time, Philly lawyers who wrote Finley letters had
never spoken with their clients, contacted the trial lawyer or obtained
available police files before deciding their claims had no merit.

None of those seemingly basic steps, I was surprised to learn, is required
under the law. In fact, dozens of lawyers I spoke to expressed sharply divided
opinions about the extent of their obligations to these clients.

But court-appointed lawyers are not working unsupervised. Judges are largely
in charge of appointing them to cases, and those same judges are supposed to
make sure they’re doing a timely and diligent job.

I noticed that judges continued to assign lawyers more cases even after
appeals courts flagged serious issues with their work. And when it came to
Finley letters, judges accepted almost all of them over the three years of
cases I reviewed, despite the lawyers’ minimal investigative efforts. Some of
the letters they approved contained obvious factual errors or even named the
wrong client.

Last fall, after Palumbo gave the lawyer a copy of a Finley letter, the lawyer
followed the template. His no-merit brief said that his client’s claim could
not be considered because he’d missed his filing deadline. The bulk of the
document was, in fact, identical to the other lawyer’s brief.

Palumbo, who didn’t respond to my requests for comment, accepted the Finley
letter anyway, let the lawyer drop the client and dismissed the claim.

### Who Judges Judges?

I thought a fair way to evaluate judges would be to look at the rulings of the
Pennsylvania’s Superior Court, the state’s appeals court that hears hundreds
of challenges to judges’ rulings on post-conviction matters each year.

And boy, did the Superior Court have thoughts on how judges are handling post-
conviction cases.

In one withering opinion, a judge bemoaned an “embarrassing saga” of deficient
lawyering that a Berks County judge had tolerated. Another derided a Philly
judge and the five attorneys she’d appointed who all missed appeals deadlines,
writing, “As Hall of Fame manager Casey Stengel said of the hapless 1962 New
York Mets, ‘Can’t anybody here play this game?’”

After logging hundreds of rebukes laid out in Superior Court opinions by hand,
I asked some colleagues with data skills to help identify as many of these
cases as possible across the last 14 years, the time frame for which opinions
were reliably posted online.

![A screengrab of text from a court opinion document that reads, in part, “By
this Court’s count, at least five attorneys have now abandoned Sanchez. … We
emphasize our disapproval of the deficient representation Sanchez has been
subjected to prior to this appeal.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/image-3_highlight.jpg?w=1149)In an excerpt from a
court opinion, a judge mentions that at least five attorneys had abandoned a
client. Obtained by ProPublica

We found that the appeals court flagged more than 250 cases in which judges
didn’t intervene as lawyers provided what the court labeled ineffective
representation: “sandbagging” a client at a hearing, stonewalling a petitioner
who’d mailed two dozen letters to the lawyer’s office or filing boilerplate
appeals so vague that they doomed their clients’ cases. In hundreds more
cases, judges failed to appoint a lawyer at all, held hearings where
petitioners went unrepresented or allowed a lawyer to drop a case, leaving the
client stranded on appeal. More than 200 times, they oversaw lawyers who
abandoned clients, tanking their appeals or stalling their cases for years.

“Judges are in a terrific position to be able to prevent these kinds of
injustices,” said Marissa Boyers Bluestine, a longtime post-conviction lawyer
who now works at the University of Pennsylvania’s law school.

The scathing reversals aside, the Superior Court affirms about 80% of lower-
court rulings. That’s expected given the strict deadlines and complicated
rules about how appeals must be filed. The appeals court is also required to
defer to the lower court’s factual decisions. And when it reverses due to an
error, the recourse is generally limited to ordering a do-over or, on rare
occasions, instructing the lower court to explore sanctions. In one opinion,
the court resorted to using boldface to call out an egregious failure: “The
PCRA court did **nothing** in this case for 20 years.” Then, it told the lower
court to try again.

![A smiling bald man with a gray goatee and eyeglasses hugs a woman to his
left, whose eyes are closed. Another man in a suit is to his right, and a
second woman looks up at him from the bottom right corner of the
image.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/VGZV3CQ4XFF5LN52OQ77RWWLGU.jpg?w=2560)Marissa Boyers
Bluestine leaves court with her newly exonerated client, Willie Veasy, center,
in 2019. At the time, she was working for the Pennsylvania Innocence Project.
She said judges have a duty to report unethical lawyering. Heather Khalifa/The
Philadelphia Inquirer

Judges do have the authority — and, in fact, an obligation under state rules —
to make disciplinary referrals. Because complaints are confidential, there is
no way to know how often they do so. But only six lawyers in the last decade
have been publicly sanctioned for work on court-appointed post-conviction
cases.

Judicial discipline is even rarer. No lower-court judge in at least a decade
has been publicly disciplined for mishandling a post-trial matter. Judges who,
according to the Superior Court, exhibited biases, imposed vindictive
sentences or improperly denied recusal requests remained on the bench.

Even after the Superior Court raised alarms, more than 100 cases ricocheted
between the appeals court and county judges two, three, four or more times, as
judges [repeated
errors](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/superior/out/J-A07027-24m%20-%20106021539275868192.pdf)
or [reappointed
lawyers](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/superior/out/J-S37040-24m%20-%20106316281305020975.pdf)
to cases [they’d already
mishandled](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/superior/out/J-S40005-20jo%20-%20104776189135315290.pdf).

One such case played out after Jefferson County’s only judge, John Foradora,
sentenced a woman to up [to 22 years in
prison](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/superior/out/J-S36018-15m%20-%201022773805011079.pdf)
for passing two narcotics pills in prison. Her lawyer failed to object to or
appeal the lengthy sentence. After she filed a PCRA, the Superior Court found
that her lawyers’ inaction enabled the  “[unduly harsh and clearly
unreasonable](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/superior/out/Opinion%20%20ReversedVacatedRemanded%20%2010377716944400986.pdf)”
punishment to stand. But each time the Superior Court reversed, Foradora again
imposed a lengthy term. After three such reversals, the woman wound up serving
more than eight years. Foradora said through a court spokesperson that he was
unable to comment.

Shannon McDonald, an attorney in the Philly suburbs, said that “some judges
don’t consider PCRA a priority.”

She described waiting as a petition languished on a Delaware County judge’s
desk for two years, until her client had finished his sentence and been
released from prison. Then, the judge finally ruled, dismissing the claim.

### The Finley Problem

Like lawyers, judges I’ve spoken with seem to be divided on their obligations,
especially when it comes to the no-merit letters known as Finley letters. The
state Supreme Court says that when a lawyer submits a Finley letter, the judge
needs to conduct a review of the merits of the case.

Attorney Rob Perkins, who leads the nonprofit Allegheny Lawyers Initiative for
Justice, told me that while he’s encountered some judges who take post-
conviction matters seriously, others seem to view them as a nuisance. He said
several lawyers told him that they were afraid that if they litigated cases
too aggressively, judges would withhold future assignments. The no-merit
letter becomes the simplest path forward: “When a judge is handed a no-merit
letter that sounds good, I think their inclination is to accept that the
attorney did their job.”

![A man in a gray suit stands with his hands crossed in front of a set of
stairs in a dimly lit historic building.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/RS3630558_FINLEY-FUNDING-004.jpg?w=2560)Rob Perkins,
an attorney and founder of Allegheny Lawyers Initiative for Justice, says some
court-appointed lawyers fear that litigating post-conviction cases
aggressively would be bad for business. Justin Merriman/The Philadelphia
Inquirer

Superior Court opinions reflect this pattern as well. In my review, I found
hundreds of cases overruling lower-court judges who accepted flawed Finley
letters. The appeals court noted that lawyers claimed, incorrectly, that their
clients had missed filing deadlines, rejected legitimate claims as meritless
or failed to notice that their clients were serving illegal sentences.

In dozens of cases, judges approved defective Finley letters that did not
fulfill basic rules, such as including a notification to the client or
addressing all the claims the client wanted to raise.

Several judges told me that Finley letters serve an important purpose, in
shutting down frivolous challenges that waste resources.

“Not all [claims] have merit,” Judge John J. Mead of Erie said. “A lot of them
initially you could look at and make a determination [as to] whether or not
it’s going to require a hearing.”

I’ve noticed that the system makes accepting Finley letters the simplest
choice for judges. A judge who rejects a Finley letter [must either find a new
lawyer](https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/pa-superior-court/1580983.html)
willing to take the case, or force the same lawyer to pursue a matter they
previously deemed meritless.

Judges who take that path risk pitting a lawyer against his own client, the
Superior Court wrote in one recent case, finding the judge’s actions resulted
in the denial of a man’s right to counsel. His lawyer, forced to handle a
hearing after writing a Finley letter, treated it “[more like a cross-
examination](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/superior/out/J-A09023-25m%20-%20106432619318613092.pdf)
of a witness that [he] does not believe than a direct examination of his
client.”

Jon Auritt, who retired after more than 50 years as a lawyer in Delaware
County, said that these failures stem from a common cause: Instead of working
independently, lawyers are beholden to the local judges who appoint them.

Even if judges are not as explicit as Palumbo was with their instructions,
Auritt said, their message is often clear: “The judges are never incentivized
to appoint a lawyer who might earnestly find a reason to overturn the
conviction.”

### How We Analyzed Appeals Court Opinions

To identify cases in which Pennsylvania appeals court judges reversed or
vacated lower court rulings on Post Conviction Relief Act cases, we compiled
about 19,000 opinions from 2011 through July 2026 published on the
Pennsylvania’s Superior Court website. The documents were identified by a
keyword search for “PCRA.”

We used artificial intelligence to identify cases in which the appeals court
took issue with judges’ errors and lawyers’ failings in lower-court
proceedings. To make the AI classifications as accurate as possible, we first
read and classified about 500 of the 19,000 opinions. We then tested the
classifications of multiple AI prompts against these 500 classifications, to
make sure they were giving us accurate results. Finally, we ran the prompt
with the best results against the rest of the documents.

Every AI classification was checked against an AI-written summary of the
opinion, or against the opinion itself. Finally, we manually checked a random
sample of 50 AI summaries to confirm that AI accurately summarized the
corresponding opinions.

The post [Lawyers in This State Are Allowed to Ghost Clients for Years. Why
Don’t More Judges Stop Them?](https://www.propublica.org/article/post-
conviction-legal-system-finley-judges-pennsylvania) appeared first on
[ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
